p:
Okay and uhm, as of the Preliminary Plan, approximately $450 million is budgeted in each Fiscals 2026 and 2027 for street

outreach. Spending under the prior Administration increased significantly hitting approximately $370 million in Fiscal 2025. Despite the investments over the past several years, unsheltered homelessness persists. How will your Administration approach effectively serving this population while balancing the fiscal implications?

Thank you for the question and I’ll start again and then if others want to add. Uhm, as I mentioned earlier, I think uhm, the work to house people that are unhoused, I mean you know very few New Yorkers are of course outside but those who are, we want to do our best work to bring them inside. I think the Mayor’s switch to having the Department of Homeless Services lead the way is the right uhm, it’s the right role. I think working across our partners in Health and Hospitals, uhm on issues of mental illness and substance use services and just really trying to wrap our arms around those folks who are staying outside and offer them - offer them what they need. And so, I think the additional staff will help along with strong coordination along with the right folks taking the lead and making sure that we are able to make offers that people will accept.

Again, a challenging issue but one I look forward to taking on.

Thank you so much and I’d like to acknowledge that we’ve been joined by Council Member Cabán on Zoom. Uhm, okay, I’d like to move into uhm, SNAP, EBT Chip Cards and state funding. So, theft of SNAP benefits is an epidemic across the United States and one of the major ways criminals steal funds is by card skimming. Using illegal devices to copy personal account information when people swipe their EBT cards. At the March 3, 2026 quarterly community partners call, HRA stated that in the state's 30 day amendment to the proposed budget, $1.8 million in state funding was added statewide with $700,000 earmarked for New York City’s implementation of chip technology for EBT cards. Will this funding be added to the Executive Plan?

Sure, I can take that question. Uhm, so the funding in the state budget is actually for the state to uh cover the cost of the transition to EBT cards with chips. Uhm, the state is the uh, does all of those EBT cards, so the funding in the state budget is actually to do that actual trans- you know transition with a vendor, so I imagine that that

funding is meant to support a vendor to transition the EBT cards to chip cards so that everything will be far more secure and we won’t have as many instances of individuals having their benefits skimmed.
And uhm, has the state provided guidance on the implementation and timeline of chip technology across the state?
Uh, they have not yet given us a definitive timeline but I do know that it is something they are uh trying to work on as quickly as possible.
Are you aware of retailers in the city who currently accept SNAP EBT cards but will not be able to accept payment from the new SNAP chip cards?

Uhm, I am not aware of that but we will uh obviously work closely with our colleagues at OTDA to make sure that they are providing the right information to individuals in case stores do need to you know look at a change in technology to be able to take the chip card.

Okay and then there are also some concerns about the new chip card that I’m going

to toss over to Council Member Avilés to get into. Thank you. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you so much Chair. On those particular cards, uhm, we understand because the chips are uhm, connected to uh financial federal regulations that there are potential vulnerabilities for immigrant New Yorkers particularly in this context, which is something we considered when we developed the IDNYC, right? Which is why the chips were not part of there - have you explored deeply those vulnerabilities in this political context and what did you -

So, we will bring that back to the oversight of OTDA, as they are actually the ones who oversee the chip cards and the determination of it. Uhm, uh and we will speak with them about you know what had they looked in and are there security measures that they are considering to ensure that people remain safe, which is a main concern for us as well. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great, it is a huge issue in our communities. Uhm, and we want to make sure that people get the benefits that they depend on so profoundly but at the same time, they should not be

ensnared and in definite detention and deportation because of their status. Thank you.

Thank you Council Member. Okay, as of December 2024, the state is no longer receiving federal reimbursement for stolen benefits. As part of the state budget, there is a proposal to create a victims compensation fund for those who have had their benefits stolen through skimming. What is HRA doing to support skimming victims and would you support a state compensation fund?

Certainly, so as you mentioned, the ability to reimburse you know SNAP skimming was stopped by the federal government. Uhm, I can’t say that you know since the beginning of the ability to replace benefits. HRA did work to replace over $50 million in benefits to individuals who submitted claims to us. We can still take claims from individuals who have had their cash assistance benefits skimmed. So, I encourage anyone who has had any of their cash assistance benefits skimmed to still submit that to us because we are able to reimburse those funds and we are very much open to working with our state colleagues on identifying

other funds that can replace benefits for individuals who had them stolen by somebody.

Great, thank you. Uhm, okay the closing of Bellevue Men's Shelter and Intake Site. The Administration recently announced it will be temporarily shutting down the Bellevue Men’s Shelter and Intake Center by mid-March. Sites on East 3rd Street and Bowery and Manhattan will assume shelter intake in Bellevue’s 250 single male residents will be rehoused beginning May 1st at shelters to be determined. Can you tell me more about how this decision was made and the logistics of shutting down Bellevue and relocating residents?

Sure, thank you for the question. Uhm and as you all know, that location at 30th Street has been the front door to the homeless services for many years in New York City and so, I don’t think anyone takes lightly that a move would need to happen. As folks also probably know, uhm, that building has been in disrepair for many years and while the city has attempted to keep up with the maintenance, it has just become a time when that can’t be done piecemeal anymore and we need to find a

safer place for the people we serve and our employees as well. And so, we’ve been working with partners on that transition. So, as of Sunday I think, March 16th, uhm, we no longer have assessment beds in 30th Street and that transition went well. Intake and assessment is still happening onsite. Uhm, of course, we will continue to have staff long after the transition who can help to direct people to other resources up to the new sites. We expect that for some time, people will continue to see that site as a resource and we will continue to staff it so that people may get to intake and assessment sites throughout the city.

Thank you and have you identified which shelters will be rehousing Bellevue residents and if so, can you tell me how you chose the new sites and do they have the same support services and accessibility as Bellevue?
Uhm, I can start but I want to make sure I am fully understanding the question.
Sure.

So, there’s the issue of intake and assessment and I can talk about that. And then there is the issue of where people are being sheltered for

that short period and I might uhm, uhm, take some support to make sure I’m answering that correctly. And so, I think uhm, yes the DHS team as well as other teams have assessed a variety of sites that would meet the needs for intake and assessment and we believe that the sites that uhm, we have chosen offer comparable and better intake and assessment accessibility to the folks who we’d be serving there and are working with our partners at Project Renewal and others to make sure that there’s continuity of care for the clients that they’re serving in those spaces as well. And let me turn to my colleagues and see what I might have missed and if I misstated anything, please feel free.
From what I’ve heard, I think you’ve covered most of it, if not all of it.

Yeah and I was just going to confirm that and say that uhm, uh, the assessment beds have been transitioned to uh sites in Brooklyn. Uhm, but uhm and you know as the Commissioner said, those you know, those have already been transitioned out. So, uhm, you know we’re fully on the path to uh

taking on what is going to be a difficult transition, obviously away from 30th Street.

Okay, thank you and uhm how many substance use or mental health treatment beds uhm did Bellevue have and how many individuals are currently housed in these beds? And has DHS identified which shelters will rehouse these individuals and how you’ll ensure there isn’t a gap in the specialized care they’re receiving?

Thank you for the question. Uhm, Bellevue served as our assessment and overnight uhm compliment of beds. So, there were no program beds there. So, once somebody was assessed, if the determination was they needed a substance abuse bed, they were placed in a substance abuse shelter.
Okay, separate from the site.
From 30th Street, correct.

Okay, will any of the new need funding added in the Preliminary Plan for shelter costs go toward housing, services or staffing for the shelters taking in the Bellevue residents and will any go towards the intake sites that will be taking over for Bellevue?

Uhm, yes, the positions that were added will go towards uhm, these efforts. I don’t know that we uhm, that I have the information on which ones go where but we can get back to you with that when we give you the breakdown of the 146.
Okay, thank you and do you plan to add additional funding or headcount for these sites in future plans?
Thank you. I believe the additional headcount of the 146 should address the need but I think when we look at the breakdown uhm, I think that we’ll find that it’s sufficient.
Okay, uhm, sufficient by your standards?
Well, when we take a very centralized, complex program that existed at Bellevue for many years and we have to decentralize it, we did need to stand up essentially multiple intake programs.
Right.
So, that’s where the additional headcount is. We believe the 146 should be sufficient to operate intake in the disbursed way that we had to approach it.
Okay, thank you. Just give me one second. Let me turn it over to Council Member Brewer for a second.

Thank you. This may have been worked out but Project Renewal was hysterical about the timeframe. Has that been worked out where it’s not as fast and you have more time at their facilities in Lower East Side? And, they have a clinic there, uhm, they want to make sure it retains because it’s very hard to restart it etc., etc., etc., since I am swamped with phone calls.
Yeah, thank you and we’re very grateful to the partners at Project Renewal. We know this is not something that they’ve had a lot of warning about and something that they’ve had to work closely -
That’s putting it mildly but yes.

Closely with us. We uh, we also have deadlines of doing intake and assessment as of May 1st uhm in the new sites. And so, we’re working closely with Project Renewal on programs that can stay in space and programs that might be better off perhaps in an additional space. Uhm, so we’re

working with state partners on the substance use treatment program, uhm, which again, I think we’ve worked out with them can stay and that’s space, so those folks will be stable and then to your point, there’s an outpatient clinic that we’re working with them on as well as a federally qualified health center in our Article 28 site that we see as really integral to the intake and assessment function and look forward to working with them. Uhm, certainly this plan is still in flux. There are state partners involved. There are - there’s Project Renewal and uhm, I think the important thing to know is that we’re all working really hard to make sure that we can - where transitions need to be made, uhm, make sure that they’re done safely and with care and, and support those clients going forward.
Do you think the federally qualified health center will be okay to stay there or are you still working that out? Because that is very hard to replicate.

We absolutely wanted to stay there and in fact, again, see it as a really integral part of that intake and assessment function, getting people connected to services. Uhm, the things we’re

working through are construction issues. How do we build out the intake and assessment components of that program and keep the Article 28 clinic intact? Those are the kinds of issues we’re working through right now.
Thank you.

And thank you Council Member Brewer. Uhm, I was getting to that line of questioning next but also just want to you know state- state for the record that uhm, the beds that are there currently at the 3rd Street site that are operated by uhm Project Renewal, uhm, are really unique and have unique needs and the people who are residents there and so, you know we want to make sure that we’re doing everything to keep those programs and services whole and I don’t know uhm, and this is -I’m actually saying, I do not know uhm, you know whether the move is going to allow those services to stay whole and I think, uhm as Council Member Brewer mentioned, the federally qualified health uhm center is a particular concern because I don’t know if that money can actually be moved into a different location, physical location. So, those are things that we want to make sure you all are talking as

Project Renewal about. Thank you. Okay, uhm, DHS vacancy rate. In July 2025, DHS’s actual headcount was 1,733 and it has been steadily declining every month since. As of January 2026, DHS has a vacancy rate of 27 percent, the highest it has been in the last three years. Why has DHS's headcount been declining over the last few months?

Uhm, thank you for that question. Uhm, so, when you look at this period of time, there are a few things happening that kind of challenge how we look at headcount. First, you know we moved the housing services division from DHS to HRA. So, you would see that actual headcount from one agency to the other.
And how many was that, do you know?
Oh, sorry, it was 107.
Thank you. And you said that went from DHS to HRA?
Correct.
Okay, so those - do those 107 positions represent the 27 percent vacancy rate?

No, so the 27 percent vacancy rate is also - a lot of that is driven from the new

needs that we received in the uhm, uh Preliminary Budget. So, if you were to you know remove those, the vacancy rate is probably closer to 14 percent.
Okay, still high, I would argue.
Of course.
Uhm, and so, just going back to the transfer then. What is the actual and budgeted headcount for the Housing Administration Program?
Give me one second, I’m sorry. Housing services, uh you know uh -

While they’re looking for that, I can say for rental assis- for the Rental Assistance program right, uh the headcount that we have is uhm, 161 but I would caution to think that is the only number of people who are actually focused on moving people out of shelter. Specifically around City FHEPs. There are many other staff both internal to our agency, as well as in partnership with our providers that actually work along the continuum of moving people out of shelter. So, I just would caution that that is not the only number of people focused on that work and that it is really focused

specifically on rental assistance. There are additional staff who obviously work in the affordable and supportive housing side of our operations that connect people to other types of permanent housing. And we can, if we need to, get back to you with the total number.
Yeah, I’m sorry, we will have to get back to you. I’m sorry.
Oh, okay. What I’m trying to get at is whether or not the budgeted headcount was revised for the Preliminary Plan to account - bless you - to account for the transfer of this program.

The transfer uhm, happened in uhm, the - the budgeted headcount had moved prior to uhm, the November budget or moved in the November budget but the actual headcount moved uhm, later. So, you’re sort of - we’re seeing a sort of a disconnect between when the budgeted headcount was moved. Only because we had to move them as part of uhm, financial plans and when the actual heads moved, which was later in the fall.
Okay, uhm, what is DHS doing to fill vacant positions and to reduce the attrition rate amongst staff?

Uhm, thank you yeah. That’s a great question. So, uhm, they are - our Human Resources Administration has a number of initiatives that they’ve taken to try to reduce the staff, uhm, the vacancies in staff. I mean, on an internal level and at the higher levels, we’re working to ensure that all of our positions are posted and that staff have an opportunity for growth within the organization. Uhm, when we are looking to bring in staff from outside of the organization, we are doing the traditional civil service hiring pools. Uhm, we post everything on our jobs website and try to advertise our positions outside of just the city’s website. Uhm, we’ve done numerous career fairs. We’ve collaborated with HRA’s career services division, done hiring hauls across the city. Uhm, and we’ve also worked within our office of marketing to create recruitment videos for uhm positions that are hard to recruit.
Okay and what would you say is uhm, an acceptable or ideal vacancy rate? If not, zero.

Yeah, I would say as close to zero as possible. Uhm, it will never be you know zero and it takes time to recruit new staff but uh, I’m certain this agency wants to have everybody on board that we can and also, for the benefit of the other staff who are here, who are taking on so much work on behalf of people. And so, while it’s difficult to attract uhm talent and it’s - and of course, I suspect this bureaucracy like all are challenging to work through. Uh, I think it’s a great opportunity to look at that process, streamline it as much as possible and get folks uh, in the door. So, I would say we would be striving to have that be as low as possible.

Okay, uhm, okay, on February 19th, DHS released an action plan for the integration for asylum seekers into the DHS system. The plan laid out the following goals: Close the last emergency asylum shelter. Bring single adult shelters into compliance with capacity limits and

comply with regulations requiring families with children to have access to cooking facilities. The plan mentions that within the next six months, DHS will open several new shelters, which were delayed by the previous administration. Can you tell me how many shelters are set to open and who the shelter providers are?

Sure, we’d love to. We’re really excited about the new shelters. Uhm, while folks are finding the specific information for you all, I’ll just say I was at a ribbon cutting for Magnolia Gardens last week and it’s a beautiful space built with the nonprofit and community, working together. You know those are the kinds of spaces we want to be able to move our families and others into. Places with services on site that fit the fabric of the community. It was just a wonderful opportunity to see those kinds of - that kind of shelter open and uhm, while I’m sure there’s always concerns when shelters are cited. What I saw there that day was so much community excitement for the space. There’s community rooms that could even be used I think by - by community members and so, just a real celebration.
I was sorry to miss that - that ribbon cutting but I’ll be visiting Magnolia Gardens soon.
Thanks Commissioner and Chair for the question. I was conferring with Chief Gonzalez. We know the sites. We know the addresses. We’ll have to get back to you on the providers.
Okay uhm and what about a breakdown of the populations that will be served. The facility types, the boroughs, and how many residents these shelters are able to house?
Yes, I can certainly answer. The population will be single men. So, these sites are opening to absorb the clients that are being transferred out the last remaining Kirk site.
Okay and after the opening of these additional shelter sites, that are already in the pipeline. Do you anticipate needing more shelter sites?

We’re constantly evaluating. Part of our large capacity management plan and the third item that you mentioned from that 45 day plan is to ensure that families are out of hotels that don’t have cooking facilities. So, that’s uhm a task

and in order to move families out of hotels, we need a robust pipeline. So, we’re continuing to identify high quality, safe, uhm, facilities to uhm allow us to exit hotels.
And uhm, do you know how many you might need? Like how many shelter sites?

I think we’d need to get back to you. The number changes as we go, right. So, when that plan was established, the census was a certain number. We know how many families were in as of the day. It’s something we’re constantly monitoring and I mentioned earlier, we work with uhm, our colleagues at OMB on the shelter projections to kind of tie what the expected census will be to the beds we’re going to need to have available at that time.

Okay. The action plan states that goals will be met in part by converting some families with children, hotel units for use by single men. How many families with children, hotel units are there currently and how many can be converted for use by single men?
Yeah, we’ll have to get back to you on the total number of family hotel units. Uhm, we don’t want to give you the incorrect number.
Okay, I just want to state for the record that we shared all of these questions with you all in advance and we’re hoping to have the numbers shared here today. So, it’s a lot of follow up.
We’ll work on that.

Uhm, one thing, I want to go back to very quickly about uhm Magnolia Gardens, which as you mentioned Commissioner is a great new facility. Uhm, the provider however, did mention that funding was cut for the PETS program and I think when folks first started talking about the PETS program, it was probably something that was, uhm, undervalued. Uhm, and people didn’t realize or understand how important PETS can be and are to families and especially those experiencing trauma and domestic violence and things of that nature. So, uhm, it seems to be a much more uhm widespread or robust program across the shelter system. And so, uh, do

you know anything about the funding for the PETS program specifically at Magnolia Gardens?
I will need to get back to you about the specific funding there.
That one I sprung on you, so I’m going to allow it.

But I certainly agree that we shouldn’t ask people to make hard choices about the people and the animals that they love. Uhm, and so, as long as we can create a safe environment for everyone staying there uhm, we should do that whenever we can.

Okay, great, thank you so much. Uhm, okay and then going back to the asylum seekers in DHS system. Uh, where do you plan to move the approximately 8,100 families with children currently in hotel shelters and how will you minimize disruption to these families' lives and to the children's schooling? I know you talked about uhm, you know doing everything we can and identifying new sites and of course we know, everybody knows we have a crisis of housing and shelter here in New York City but for the families with children specifically, uhm, what’s your plan to minimize disruption?

Okay, thank you for the question uhm Chair. Uhm, first and foremost, uhm outside of any need for an emergency transfer, we are looking to ensure that families are not transferred. Families with school age children until after the school year whenever possible. Uhm, that’s one of our approaches and I just want to uhm, confirm for you the number of family hotel units that we have, 11,084.
11,084. Thank you so much.

And just to build on that point because I’ve asked about it a little bit as well. So, in addition to whenever possible not changing - asking younger children to - children that are school age to change schools.
Right.
Uhm, I know we’re providing transportation if people want to stay in home schools. We believe in obviously the - the education stability and making sure there’s continuity there.

Great, thank you and given that asylum seekers often have unique needs different from the general DHS population, how do you plan to serve them after they’ve been integrated into the

DHS, while also keeping them safe from immigration customs enforcement officers?

Sure, thank you for the question Chair. Uhm, throughout the process of integrating asylum seekers into our general shelter population, uhm, everyone is treated the same. So, everyone is assessed in the same way. Service plans are delivered in the same way and the specific needs around asylum seekers, whether it’s legal or immigration services, get added to the service plan, just as they would if child care was needed or employment services were needed. We partner with the Mayor’s Office of Immigration Affairs to make sure we have the most current and client forward uhm, facing materials and resources. Our providers, uhm just like they would for medical providers or employment programs, are responsible for making sure they have a network of resources to refer clients in need too.

Thank you. Uh, I’d like to acknowledge that we’ve been joined by Millennium High School from here in Manhattan. Welcome students from Millennium High School. This is a Preliminary Budget hearing for the General Welfare Committee, which has oversight over Department of Social Services, which

includes the Department of Homeless Services and uh, the Human Resources Administration. So, welcome to City Hall. Uhm, okay, disability and aging accomodations in shelter. As the former Chair of the Council’s Committee on Aging, I’ve seen how older New Yorkers have unique needs and I’m concerned about uhm, and how DHS is meeting the needs of this population in the shelter system. Can you provide an estimate of how many people in shelters are 60 years old or older?
Thank you for the question. We will get you an estimate of the number of people in shelter 60 or older.
Uhm, okay, you don’t have that?
Not at my fingertips, no.
Okay.
Apologies.
What specialized support services does DHS provide to this population?

We have a few sites uhm, that are designed specifically for this uhm population. Uhm, they tend to be lower density. They tend to be

more accessible for those with mobility or chronic uh medical issues. Uhm, some of the providers that operate these sites also have their own housing programs, supportive housing programs and we ensure that working - we’re working with our HRA partners and other city agencies for any housing options that are dedicated specifically to uhm, this population.
And what specialized support services are available to shelter residents with disabilities?

So, yeah, uhm, our Office of Disability Affairs is always available to assist our shelter providers with any needs uhm, that they feel that they need to assist a client in order to meet to make sure that they have full access to services that we offer. We have a robust reasonable accommodation process that allows uhm, at the people we serve to request accommodations, whether it’s a change in policy or procedure or additional time with an application or having information read to them, to make sure that they’re fully aware and participating in their service plan.

And what does uhm, what does the review process for those requests look like? And

based on what you’re saying, basically the information is presented to the person and then they would you know- know what their options are or are there cases where people are asking specifically for specific accommodations?
We certainly get uhm, those instances as well as it’s our responsibility also to pay attention to proactively uhm see if they’re -
Identify needs.

Yes, visible and apparent needs. So, for example, if somebody comes in and applies for shelter uhm, and we’re looking for a placement, we’re going to look for one for somebody in a wheelchair, who uses a wheelchair, then elevator.
Right and some disabilities are invisible-
Right.
But I recognize that for those that are visible you do your best at intake.

Right and for those that are invisible or for things that arise when somebody is placed in shelter. The individual who is in receipt of shelter, can apply directly for reasonable

accommodation on their own by submitting a form. The shelter staff is there also to assist them uhm in completing the form and it’s likely that we’re going to need documentation. So, shelter staff is also there to help them gather that documentation and make sure it gets to us.
Okay, uhm, would lack of documentation prevent one from receiving a reasonable accommodation?
It depends. It depends on what the - the need is.
Okay, can you give me an example of when somebody might be denied a reasonable accommodation for lack of -
For lack of documentation?
Yeah.

So, if somebody in shelter uhm, submits a reasonable accommodation, they need their own unit and their own bathroom. Uhm, we would ask for medical documentation that would indicate that that is in fact a need.
Okay.
And if that documentation was not provided, uhm, the reasonable accommodation will likely be denied.
Okay, at that time? But there’s an opportunity for -
And again, the shelter staff is responsible for helping uhm, people to secure the documents that they need.
Okay. How many DHS shelters are wheelchair accessible?
I’ll get back to you on that.
Okay and uhm, does DHS take age and disability into account when placing clients into shelters?
Yes, as I mentioned, we do have a few shelters that are uhm designed.
Specific, hmm, hmm.

Yeah, so as uhm, if there are available beds there, we would certainly place them as long as it was appropriate. And as those sites uhm have permanent placements and beds become available, we would be transferring appropriate folks in.
Okay and I assume you take into consideration the availability of community services and amenities and access to public transportation and other factors that those vulnerable populations would need?
Yes.

How does DHS coordinate with agencies such as uh NYC Aging and the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities to better serve older adults and people with disabilities who are experiencing homelessness.

We’re constantly engaging with our sister agency partners around best practices, any new services. Uhm, pushing for additional housing supports. Uhm, making sure that our providers are aware of all the services that are offered by our sister agencies as well.

Thank you and uhm I’m going to go to Council Member Avilés for a few more questions and then I have a question here from Council Member Thomas-Henry whose joined us online but unfortunately, we don’t have quorum at the moment and so, I’ll have to ask her question for her.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you so much Chair. Thank you uhm to the whole team for your work and being here today. Uhm, so I want to talk a little bit about uhm the Immigration Legal Services. Uhm, in the Preliminary Plan includes $6.7 million of city funding added in Fiscal ‘26 and $21.3 million added in Fiscal ‘27, $20.9 million added in Fiscal ‘28. Uhm, and continuing on in outyears. Uhm, can you tell us what this funding is for specifically and what programs are going to be impacted by the additional funding?

So, it actually - it supports a variety of immigration services across different uh programs and different agencies. So, it will support IOI, which is at uh HRA, under our Office of Civil Justice. It also supports - COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Can you tell me how much for each program, what would be the breakdown? So, IOI at HRA at what amount?

Okay, so we’ll provide the breakdown on each specific agency. Uhm, if they don’t have it in there but IOI then the Office, End GBV, End Gender Based Violence is also has programs that will receive some of that funding. Uhm, uh, our

colleagues at MOIA also receive some of that funding. Additionally, we have a low wage worker protection program at HRA that will also receive some of the additional funding and we’ll get back to you with the specific amounts for each one of those programs, but it crosses a variety of programs that focus on supporting uh, individuals who may experience immigration issues that need legal representation. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great, so when you report back, we’d love to see the breakdown across and then across years.

Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you. In terms of the uhm, the Preliminary Plan also includes uhm $11.6 million in city funding added to the baseline starting in Fiscal ‘27 for immigration legal support centers operated by MOIA. Are there specific MOIA legal services or programs that the funding is for? And what providers will be part of this program? Also, will there be a new RFP?
